title: Bitcoin analysis: More volume, but less downside damage (possible dip?)
body: Bitcoin's rebound from $55,130 has some encouraging short-term evidence behind it. Still, the broader Bitcoin outlook is not yet bullish again, and the $62,000-$62,640 area may help decide whether this is a recovery in progress or just a bounce inside a larger downtrend. Bitcoin's rebound from $55,130 on November 21 to roughly $61,500 on November 22 is notable for more than one reason. Yes, the move was large, about 11% from low to rebound high. But the more useful clue may be what happened between trading volume and price damage. Bitcoin analysis: more volume, but less downside damage On November 20, Bitcoin fell sharply on about 38,126 BTC of volume. On November 21, volume rose further to about 48,558 BTC, yet the market failed to stay down. After printing the $55,130 low, Bitcoin recovered and closed the day near $60,216. That recent price action over this weekend is not insignificant. The footprint data suggests sellers were still aggressive, but their impact weakened. The negative sell imbalance narrowed materially from the prior day, while price finished higher. That does not prove a major bottom is in. It does suggest that heavy selling was producing less downside progress. For traders, that is often worth noticing. Sunday then added another layer. A completed four-hour candle advanced about 3.2%, and that move came with clearly positive buying pressure. That is more constructive than a simple green candle after an oversold drop.

title: New Zealand retail volumes jump 2.2% in Q3, more than four times the expected pace
body: A beat of this size is supportive for the New Zealand dollar and should firm rate expectations at the margin, since it weakens the case that NZ consumers need more help. Any boost may be short-lived, though, with global risk appetite under heavy pressure after last week's Wall Street rout. A high-beta currency like the kiwi tends to follow broader sentiment in that kind of market. Liquidity is also thinner than usual with Tokyo closed, which can exaggerate the first move in either direction. ---- New Zealand consumers didn't just recover in the third quarter, they outran forecasts by a wide margin, putting a firmer floor under the growth outlook. Summary: NZ retail sales volumes rose 2.2% q/q in the third quarter, seasonally adjusted, against a 0.5% consensus. Second-quarter volumes were revised to a 0.4% fall from 0.5%. Actual sales volumes rose 3.5% y/y, up from 3.3% in the second quarter. Second-quarter sales excluding vehicles had risen 0.7%, which pointed to autos as the earlier drag. The figures feed into third-quarter GDP estimates. New Zealand retail sales volumes rose far faster than expected in the third quarter, a strong signal that household spending recovered after a soft middle of the year. Statistics New Zealand data released on Monday local time showed volumes climbed a seasonally adjusted 2.2% on the quarter, more than four times the 0.5% gain economists had forecast. Actual sales volumes were up 3.5% on a year earlier.

title: Seoul readies a market fund unused since 2008 after the Kospi sinks
body: The measures give Korean stocks a policy backstop before Monday's open. Readying the fund rather than deploying it, though, leaves authorities room to hold back unless selling becomes disorderly. Looser buyback limits could help the chip heavyweights and other large caps most, since they have the cash to step in. A Bank of Korea hike on Thursday would mean tighter monetary policy while equities are falling, which could weigh on sentiment even as fiscal and regulatory authorities try to calm it. With Japan shut for a holiday, Seoul's session is likely to set the tone for Asian tech this morning, and the won will show whether foreign outflows are building. --- Meanwhile, Bessent clutching at straws: US equity rout: Bessent cautions Fed against overtightening, before its December decision --- Seoul is loading its emergency tools before Monday's open, but the measures only help if the AI sell-off stops spreading from Wall Street. Summary: South Korea's finance minister, central bank governor and top financial regulators held an emergency meeting on Sunday over possible spillover from the US stock rout. The government will immediately start preparing a stock market stabilisation fund so it can be used when needed. Local media say it would be the fund's first use since 2008. Daily share buyback limits for listed firms will be eased for three months, and an intensive three-month crackdown on illegal short selling begins.

title: US equity rout: Bessent cautions Fed against overtightening, before its December decision
body: With a quarter-point hike in December close to fully priced, Bessent's comments mainly push back against the governors (well, one, looking at you Waller!) arguing for 50 basis points. They do little to dislodge 25bp as the base case. If the equity correction deepens, the bigger risk for rate markets is that a hold gets priced back in. For oil, the administration's argument depends on crude-driven inflation fading, so softer energy prices would strengthen Bessent's case and a new spike would back the hawks. Gold has tended to fall on rising hike expectations, so any easing of that pricing could take some pressure off the metal. --- Coming today: Economic and event calendar in Asia 23 November 2026. Japanese markets are closed today. --- With Wall Street in correction and a December decision approaching, the Treasury is now openly arguing that the Fed, not the energy shock, is the bigger risk to the economy. Summary: Bessent told CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday that the Fed may be making a policy mistake if it overtightens. He cited hawkish remarks from Fed governors and a substantial tightening in financial conditions over recent months. He linked the stock market sell-off to Democratic gains in the polls, the party's stance on the AI buildout, and the Fed's tone. In CNBC interviews on 13 and 20 November, he argued against hiking hard into an easing energy supply shock and against a 50 basis point move.

title: Economic and event calendar in Asia 23 November 2026. Japanese markets are closed today.
body: Japan holiday thins out Asia Japanese markets are closed on Monday for Labor Thanksgiving Day. Tokyo equities and Japanese government bonds are not trading, and physical US Treasuries will not change hands in the Asian session. Cash Treasury trading normally runs through Tokyo hours, so it will be quiet until London opens. Treasury futures are still trading on Globex. With Japanese participants away, yen crosses may be thinner than usual, so moves can run further than the news behind them. New Zealand: retail sales expected to recover The main release in the region is New Zealand's third-quarter retail sales, due at 21:45 GMT (16:45 US Eastern) on Sunday. Consensus expects a 0.5% rise on the quarter after a 0.5% fall in the second quarter. The ex-autos measure matters more than usual this time. In the second quarter, sales excluding vehicles rose 0.7% while the headline fell. That split points to the motor vehicle category as the drag, not households cutting spending across the board. If the headline meets or beats forecast and the ex-autos number stays positive, it would suggest spending held up better through the middle of the year than the second quarter's headline implied. A miss would point the other way. Another headline fall, especially with a softer core reading, would raise new doubts about consumer spending. It would also support the view that the economy needs more help from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand.
